summary.text: The Richter scale, later renamed the local magnitude scale M_L, measures earthquake strength and was presented in 1935 by Charles Richter, working with Beno Gutenberg.
It is logarithmic: each whole-number step means ten times the measured wave amplitude and about 31.6 times the energy released.
Because of its shortcomings, most authorities now report quakes on other scales such as moment magnitude, though the news media still call them Richter values.

facts.label: Zero point aim
facts.value: Near the limit of human perceptibility

items.prompt: A quake measures magnitude 5 and an earlier one measured magnitude 3. How much larger was the measured wave amplitude of the bigger quake?

options.label: About 2 times
About 20 times
About 100 times
About 1,000 times

items.explain: Each whole step is a tenfold rise in amplitude, so two steps make ten times ten, a hundredfold increase.

items.prompt: Why did Richter choose a logarithmic scale rather than a simple linear one?

options.label: To keep every value below ten
To span the huge range of quake sizes
To match a list of building damage
Because seismographs record only logs

items.explain: Quake sizes vary enormously, and a logarithmic scale keeps that wide range of values manageable.

items.prompt: Richter's step-by-tenfold scale was modelled on a magnitude scale astronomers already used. What did theirs measure?

options.label: The brightness of stars
The distance to planets
The temperature of the Sun
The speed of comets

items.explain: Gutenberg suggested the logarithmic idea, similar to the astronomers' magnitude scale for star brightness.

items.prompt: A news site reports a huge quake as "8.8 on the Richter scale". What is most likely wrong with that label?

options.label: The number rates shaking at one town
The quake was too small to register
The value is really a moment magnitude
The scale only works for undersea quakes

items.explain: Modern values are moment magnitudes, often mislabelled as Richter, and the Richter scale becomes meaningless above about 8.

items.prompt: Two quakes have the same magnitude, yet one wrecks a city and the other is barely felt. Which difference could explain this?

options.label: Their seismograms used different paper
More stations recorded the first one
Their magnitudes were rounded differently
One focus lay much deeper underground

items.explain: Ground effects depend not only on magnitude but on distance, depth of the focus, location and local geology.

items.prompt: Richter's method relied on one particular seismograph. What happened when that instrument met a very strong earthquake?

options.label: It could not record the high values
It recorded the quake twice over
It split the quake into small ones
It worked equally well at any size

items.explain: The instrument became saturated by strong earthquakes and was unable to record high values.
